items.stem: Why is random cross-validation often too optimistic for molecular property prediction?

options.text: Structurally similar molecules can appear in both folds, leaking information
options.rationale: Correct: near-duplicates across folds inflate measured performance.

options.text: Random splitting is always the most rigorous approach
options.rationale: For molecules, scaffold or time splits are usually more realistic.

options.text: Cross-validation cannot be used in chemistry
options.rationale: It can, but the splitting strategy matters.
The bias is typically toward over-optimism, not pessimism.

items.explanation: Correct: near-duplicates across folds inflate measured performance.

items.stem: A toxicity classifier reports 95% accuracy on data where 95% of compounds are non-toxic. What is the concern?

options.text: A trivial model that always predicts non-toxic reaches the same accuracy, so accuracy is uninformative
options.rationale: Correct: with class imbalance, accuracy hides poor minority-class performance.

options.text: The model is clearly excellent and ready to deploy
options.rationale: High accuracy under imbalance can be meaningless.

options.text: Accuracy is the only metric that matters here
options.rationale: Balanced metrics such as recall and AUC are needed.

options.text: The data set is too large to evaluate
options.rationale: Size is not the issue; class imbalance is.

items.explanation: Correct: with class imbalance, accuracy hides poor minority-class performance.
